question.text: During an NFO, an investor invests Rs. 1,00,000 at the face value of Rs. 10 per unit. After 6 months, the NAV of the scheme rises to Rs. 12. If the investor had instead invested in an existing fund with NAV of Rs. 100 that also rose by 20% in the same period, which investment would have generated higher returns?

answer.text: The NFO investment would generate higher returns because units were bought at Rs. 10
The existing fund would generate higher returns because it has a proven track record
Both investments would generate the same 20% return — the starting NAV does not determine returns
The returns cannot be compared as the two funds have different NAVs

explanation.text: The Logic: NFO units are sold at the face value of Rs. 10, so Rs. 1,00,000 buys 10,000 units; at NAV Rs. 12, value = 10,000 × Rs. 12 = Rs. 1,20,000. For ongoing purchases, units are calculated as amount divided by the sale price, so Rs. 1,00,000 at NAV Rs. 100 buys 1,000 units; after a 20% rise (NAV Rs. 120), value = 1,000 × Rs. 120 = Rs. 1,20,000. Both yield a 20% return because the return depends on the percentage change in NAV from the beginning NAV to the ending NAV. The Trap: Many investors believe buying at a "low" NAV (Rs. 10 NFO) is cheaper and therefore better than buying at a higher NAV. You get more units at the lower NAV, but each unit appreciates by the same percentage, so the rupee return is the same. Note: Returns from a mutual fund investment are based on the change in NAV between the date of purchase and the date of valuation, not on the absolute level of the starting NAV.
